Household Order
HOWS-hohld OR-der
noun phrase
From Old English hūshāld (household, family under one roof) compounded with ordor (arrangement, rank), through Middle English ordre from Old French ordre, from Latin ordo (row, rank, regular arrangement); first applied to domestic hierarchical structure in Protestant Reformation commentary on the Haustafeln (household codes) of Paul’s epistles (Eph. 5–6; Col. 3–4; 1 Pet. 2–3). The compound “household order” as a theological unit emerges in Puritan domestic theology and covenant theology literature.

Biblical Definition

Household order is the God-appointed structure of authority and submission within the domestic realm—the arrangement by which the covenant home images the relationship of Christ and His church. The Scriptures do not leave domestic life unordered by divine command but assign clear roles: the husband as head, the wife as helpmeet and co-heir in submission to her husband, and children under the authority of their parents (Eph. 5:22–6:4; Col. 3:18–21). This ordering is not a concession to fallen culture but a creation ordinance predating the fall—the male was formed first and given dominion, the female was created as his suitable helper (Gen. 2:18–23; 1 Tim. 2:13).

The Apostle Paul’s Haustafeln (household codes) in Ephesians and Colossians are not cultural adaptations to first-century patriarchy but positive theological instruction grounded in creation theology and Christology: the husband’s headship is modeled on Christ’s headship over the church (Eph. 5:23), and the wife’s willing submission is modeled on the church’s submission to Christ (Eph. 5:24). The order is mutual in dignity and honor, hierarchical in authority and function—both husband and wife bear the image of God, but they bear it in differentiated ways that together constitute a domestic icon of the covenant.

The 1689 London Baptist Confession treats marriage as a covenant between one man and one woman (LBCF 25.1), and Puritan domestic theology (William Gouge, Of Domestical Duties, 1622) developed the most thorough exposition of household order in the English tradition. The godly household was called “a little church” (ecclesiola), with the husband functioning as prophet, priest, and king of his family under Christ.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) defined order as “Regular disposition or methodical arrangement; established succession; grade; class; rank; a state of peace, where law or authority is observed.” Applied to the household, this is the covenantal arrangement in which God-appointed authority and willing submission dwell together in peace.

ORDER, n. [L. ordo; Fr. ordre.] Regular disposition or methodical arrangement; a proper and established succession of things or persons.

Established succession; settled rule of proceeding; regular or methodical arrangement; observance of proper rule or authority in rank and precedence.

A state in which law or authority is observed; peace and quiet; regular government; freedom from riot or disturbance.

A rule or regulation prescribed by superior authority; a mandate, precept, or direction; a command.

In the domestic sphere: the arrangement of the household according to divinely appointed roles—authority rightly held and submission rightly rendered, so that the home becomes a picture of the covenant between Christ and His church.

Key Scripture

Eph. 5:22–24 — "Wives, submit to your own husbands as to the Lord, for the husband is the head of the wife as also Christ is the head of the church, himself the savior of the body. But as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything."

Col. 3:18–19 — "Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives and do not be embittered toward them."

Gen. 2:18 — "Then the LORD God said, “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper corresponding to him.”"

1 Tim. 3:4–5 — "He must manage his own household well, keeping his children submissive and respectful in every way — for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he take care of God’s church?"

Modern Corruption

Modern egalitarianism reads the Pauline household codes as first-century cultural accommodations to be set aside by the church, discarding the creation-grounded order in favor of a flattened, structureless domestic arrangement.

expand to see more

The primary corruption is the “cultural relativity” hermeneutic applied by evangelical egalitarians (CBE International, Christians for Biblical Equality) to the Haustafeln: the household codes were, on this reading, concessions to Roman Patria Potestas that the church must now transcend in light of Galatians 3:28. This interpretive move is circular—it presupposes that the egalitarian reading of Genesis 2 is correct in order to dismiss the plain sense of Ephesians 5, when the Apostle explicitly grounds the household order in the pre-fall creation (1 Tim. 2:13) and in Christology (Eph. 5:23–24), not in cultural convention. The result is churches that train women for eldership and men for therapeutic servility, producing homes with no ordered head and no joyful helpmeet.

A second distortion is the therapeutic inversion: complementarian language is nominally retained while the substance is surrendered—headship redefined as “servant leadership” meaning whatever the wife prefers, and submission reduced to a posture the husband must earn through performance. The biblical pattern is unconditional in its structural form even while warm, mutual, and self-giving in its spirit. The husband is called to lead as Christ leads—sacrificially—but he is nonetheless called to lead; the wife is called to submit as the church submits to Christ—willingly—but she is nonetheless called to submit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two Old English and Latin streams meet: the word for home and family, and the word for rank and arrangement, producing a phrase that captures the Reformation conviction that God structures the home as He structures the cosmos.

expand to see more

Old English hūshāld — a family or domestic unit under one roof, governed by a head; from hūs (house) + hāld (holding, keeping); the compound points to the stewardship and governance entrusted to the head of house

Latin ordo — a row, rank, series, regular arrangement; used in classical Latin for the ordering of troops, citizens, and social classes; adopted by the church for the ordering of ministry, worship, and (in Reformation commentary) the domestic sphere

Greek oikos (οἶκος) — house, household, family, temple; the Pauline Haustafeln (lit. “house tablets”) are instructions for the oikos as a social and theological unit

Puritan usage — William Gouge (Of Domestical Duties, 1622) and Richard Baxter (A Christian Directory, 1673) developed “household order” as a technical term of pastoral theology for the right government of the Christian home

Reformation Hauskirche (house-church) tradition — the ordered household as a domestic church, the husband as domestic minister, the family as a covenant unit whose internal order mirrors the order of the visible church

Usage

"The Apostle Paul’s household codes presuppose a household order given by creation and confirmed by redemption—a structure not negotiated between spouses but received from God as the pattern for covenant domesticity."

"Reformed domestic theology from Calvin to the Puritans treated household order as a matter of Christian obedience, not optional preference—the husband who abdicates his headship and the wife who usurps it both sin against the creation ordinance."

"A church that will not preach household order will eventually produce a congregation of disordered homes; the connection between ecclesial health and domestic faithfulness is axiomatic in the Reformation tradition."
